snip.t: Immune system (specifically T-lymphocytes): CD4+ T-lymphocytes are central to cell-mediated immunity, particularly against intracellular pathogens and fungi like *Pneumocystis jirovecii*.
The inflammatory component is driven by Th2-type T lymphocytes which facilitate IgE synthesis through production of IL-4 and eosinophilic inflammation through IL-5
● NHL is a diverse group of solid tumors which occurs with the malignant transformation and growth\nof B or T lymphocytes or their precursors in the lymphatic system.
T-lymphocyte defects (congenital or acquired by chemotherapy, AIDS, or malignancy) are associated with an increased risk of Listeria monocytogenes infections of the CNS.
Immune system: Macrophages (phagocytosis, granuloma formation), T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity, cytokine production), granuloma structure (caseous necrosis, fibrous cuff).
The risk of PCP significantly increases as the CD4+ T-lymphocyte count drops.
The CD4+ T-lymphocyte: The central coordinator of adaptive cell-mediated immunity.

qs.q: Which clinical feature is characteristic of T-lymphocyte defects, whether congenital or acquired via chemotherapy, AIDS, or malignancy?
o: High incidence of Streptococcus pneumoniae empyema
Increased risk of Listeria monocytogenes CNS infections
Predilection for Gram-negative enteric shunt abscesses
qs.e: T-lymphocyte defects are associated with an increased risk of Listeria monocytogenes infections of the CNS. Neisseria infections are instead linked to complement and properdin pathway deficiencies.

qs.q: A 19-year-old university student presents with fever, severe pharyngitis, generalized lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. A peripheral blood smear reveals atypical lymphocytes. What is the primary host cell type destroyed by cytotoxic T-lymphocytes in this condition?
o: Dendritic cells located in lymph nodes
Epithelial cells located in salivary glands
qs.e: Infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV induces a host response where cytotoxic T-lymphocytes appear as atypical lymphocytes to destroy EBV-infected B-cells. Epithelial cells serve as the initial site of viral replication rather than the target of CTL destruction.

qs.q: A 25-year-old man presents with a well-circumscribed, pigmented skin lesion on his trunk that has developed a symmetric, surrounding zone of depigmentation over the past two months. Histologic examination of the depigmented margin reveals a dense dermal infiltrate composed predominantly of CD8+ T lymphocytes surrounding nevus cells. What is the underlying pathophysiologic process of this finding?
o: Complement-mediated microvascular thrombosis in the dermis
Host immune response directed against melanocytes
Malignant clonal proliferation of atypical keratinocytes
Granulomatous destruction of dermal elastic fibers
qs.e: A halo nevus involves a T-cell-mediated immune response targeting shared antigens on both nevus cells and normal epidermal melanocytes. Granulomatous destruction of elastic fibers is characteristic of other dermal elastolytic conditions rather than immune-mediated depigmentation.
qs.s: Pigmentation & Melanocyte Disorders: Nevi, Freckles Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A virology student analyzes a chronic viral infection where the host liver damage is primarily driven by cytotoxic T lymphocytes attacking infected hepatocytes rather than direct viral cytopathic effects. Which virus typically exhibits this pathogenesis?
qs.e: Hepatitis B liver damage is largely immune-mediated, caused by the host's own cytotoxic T lymphocytes and inflammation rather than direct viral killing. Rhinovirus and rotavirus cause acute lytic infections rather than immune-mediated chronic hepatitis.
qs.s: Medical Virology Semester 3 Crash Revision: MCQs

qs.q: Which subtype of T lymphocytes directly targets and destroys infected or cancerous cells presenting foreign antigens?
qs.e: Cytotoxic T cells directly target and destroy infected, cancerous, or foreign antigen-presenting cells. Helper T cells assist other cells by releasing cytokines rather than directly killing targets.

qs.q: Which type of immunity is primarily mediated by T lymphocytes targeting intracellular pathogens and tumor cells?
qs.e: T lymphocytes are critical for cell-mediated immunity, whereas B lymphocytes handle humoral immunity via antibodies. Both cooperate within the adaptive immune system.

qs.q: A study of pathologic findings in the islets of Langerhans is performed. It is observed that insulitis may occur in the islets. The inflammatory infiltrate is predominantly composed of T lymphocytes. Which of the following complications is most likely to occur as a consequence of insulitis?
qs.e: An insulitis can precede the development of type I diabetes mellitus. Actually, it is rare to see it because by the time the patients present with overt diabetes mellitus, the islets are long gone. The presence of the T lymphocytes suggests an autoimmune component to the pathogenesis.

qs.q: A cytotoxic T lymphocyte kills a virus-infected cell primarily by:
o: Releasing TNF to activate the mitochondrial pathway
Producing reactive oxygen species that damage DNA
Secreting granzymes that directly activate caspases
Expressing Fas ligand to engage death receptors
qs.e: CTLs express FasL on their surface, which binds Fas on target cells, triggering the extrinsic apoptosis pathway. While CTLs also use perforin/granzymes (c is tempting), the PRIMARY and most efficient mechanism is Fas-FasL interaction. This is why Fas deficiency causes impaired viral clearance.

ai.title: T Lymphocytes and Clinical Immunology
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: T cells drive cell‑mediated immunity, coordinate cytokine responses and determine susceptibility to intracellular infections. Understanding their subsets, lab assessment and common deficits guides bedside decisions in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: T lymphocytes are mature thymic‑derived white blood cells that recognise antigen presented on MHC molecules. CD4+ helper T cells orchestrate immune responses; CD8+ cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells. Their balance is crucial for defence against viruses, intracellular bacteria, fungi and for vaccine efficacy.
b: Develop in thymus, undergo positive and negative selection
Express T‑cell receptor (TCR) with CD3 complex
Require IL‑2 for proliferation after activation

sections.p: T cells lack surface immunoglobulin; instead they display a clonally unique TCR. Subsets are defined by surface markers (CD4, CD8) and cytokine profiles (Th1, Th2, Th17, Treg).
b: Th1 → IFN‑γ, activates macrophages (important for TB, leishmaniasis)
Th2 → IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13, drives IgE and eosinophilia (asthma, helminths)

sections.p: Clinically relevant T‑cell defects are either primary (genetic) or secondary (acquired). In low‑resource East African hospitals the most common secondary deficits are HIV infection, malnutrition, and chemotherapy for cancers.
b: HIV → progressive CD4+ loss, opportunistic infections (PCP, TB, cryptococcal meningitis)
Severe malnutrition → reduced thymic output, low CD4+ counts

sections.p: Assess quantity and function of T cells. In settings without flow cytometry, surrogate clinical clues guide management.

t.b: How many functional helper T cells are present? → <200 cells/µL predicts high risk of PCP; 200‑350 cells/µL indicates need for prophylaxis against opportunists.
What is the balance of cytotoxic to helper T cells? → Low ratio (<1) suggests advanced HIV; high ratio may indicate immune reconstitution.
Is cell‑mediated immunity intact? → Anergy (no induration) points to severe T‑cell dysfunction.

sections.p: Management focuses on correcting the underlying cause, preventing opportunistic infections, and supporting immune recovery.
b: Start antiretroviral therapy (ART) promptly in HIV; monitor CD4+ rise.
Nutritional rehabilitation (protein‑rich diet, micronutrients) improves thymic output.
Prophylaxis: trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole when CD4+ <200 cells/µL; fluconazole for CD4+ <100 cells/µL in endemic areas.
Avoid high‑dose steroids unless indicated, as they further suppress T cells.

sections.p: Examiners test integration of immunology with bedside reasoning.
b: Link low CD4+ count to specific opportunistic infections.
Explain why PCP prophylaxis is started at <200 cells/µL.
Distinguish Th1‑driven diseases (TB, leishmaniasis) from Th2‑driven (helminths, allergic asthma).

whenToSeekHelp: Severe opportunistic infection (e.g., cryptococcal meningitis, disseminated TB) in a patient with known low CD4+ count
Rapid CD4+ decline >50 cells/µL in a month despite ART
Unexplained persistent fever with neutropenia and lymphopenia

faq.q: Why does PCP become common when CD4+ falls below 200 cells/µL?
faq.a: CD4+ cells are essential for recruiting macrophages and producing cytokines that control Pneumocystis; their loss impairs clearance.

faq.q: Can a normal CD4+ count rule out HIV‑related immune dysfunction?
faq.a: No; functional defects can exist early, and CD8+ expansion or high viral load may still indicate risk.

faq.q: What bedside sign suggests severe T‑cell deficiency?
faq.a: Recurrent oral thrush or chronic diarrhoea with weight loss in a young adult is a red flag.

exam: A 32‑year‑old HIV patient presents with dry cough and fever; CD4+ count is 180 cells/µL. What is the next immediate step? — Start empiric PCP prophylaxis (TMP‑SMX) and obtain sputum for Pneumocystis staining.

A malnourished child has persistent oral thrush despite antifungal therapy. Which immune parameter should you assess and why? — Measure CD4+ count; low values explain susceptibility and guide nutritional/ART interventions.

In a patient on chemotherapy for lymphoma, you note a CD4+ count of 150 cells/µL but no infections yet. What prophylactic measures are indicated? — Begin TMP‑SMX for PCP and consider fluconazole if local cryptococcal prevalence is high.

How does a Th1‑dominant response protect against intracellular bacteria, and which cytokine is pivotal? — IFN‑γ activates macrophages to kill intracellular organisms such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

A patient with severe asthma shows high eosinophil count and elevated IgE. Which T‑cell subset is driving this and what cytokine would you target? — Th2 cells; IL‑5 is key for eosinophil survival, targeted by anti‑IL‑5 agents.

Why is high-dose corticosteroid therapy contraindicated in a patient with active TB and low CD4+ count? — Steroids further suppress Th1 responses, worsening bacterial control and increasing mortality.

Explain why a CD4/CD8 ratio <1 is more prognostic than absolute CD4+ count in early HIV infection. — The ratio reflects immune dysregulation; a falling ratio predicts faster progression even when CD4+ numbers are still modest.

A refugee from a schistosomiasis‑endemic area presents with eosinophilia and cough. Which T‑cell subset is likely predominant and what does this imply for treatment? — Th2 predominance; treat with praziquantel and consider anti‑IL‑4/IL‑5 strategies if severe eosinophilic lung disease.
